items.content_html: A study using more than 30 years of atmospheric measurements estimates that oceans absorbed 35% of fossil-fuel carbon dioxide emissions from 1990 to 2019, while land ecosystems absorbed 13%. The ocean sink grew over that period, but researchers found no robust trend in the net land sink. Scientists led by a team at the University of California San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography used atmospheric oxygen and carbon dioxide measurements to assess the sinks. The results differ from many climate-model simulations. The researchers say warmer oceans could become less effective at absorbing carbon, and the data suggest growth in the ocean sink may be slowing.

items.title: [rfi.fr] COP31 climate science dispute threatens 2028 emissions progress review
items.content_html: Negotiators at COP31 in Antalya are divided over whether the U.N. climate science panel’s next assessments will be ready for the 2028 global review of emissions progress. The European Union and dozens of countries want publication before then, while Saudi Arabia, India and China support delaying the reports until 2029. The dispute concerns the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC) seventh assessment, which will examine climate change and options for adaptation and emissions cuts. Governments use the panel’s findings to assess collective progress under the Paris Agreement. A climate scientist who contributed to earlier assessments said decisions should use current rather than seven-year-old evidence. The IPCC’s October meeting ended without agreement, and the timing dispute is now part of the wider COP31 negotiations. A separate report by the Kick Big Polluters Out coalition counted 103 companies and industry groups at the summit, including 60 from the fossil-fuel sector. It said their delegations outnumbered those of several climate-vulnerable countries. Climate TRACE estimates that electrification powered by clean energy could cut global emissions by 14%, compared with 7% if fossil fuels are also used.

items.title: [phys.org] IOM chief warns climate risks could displace over 200 million
items.content_html: Amy Pope, director general of the International Organization for Migration (IOM), warned at the United Nations climate conference, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, that more than 200 million people living in highly climate-vulnerable communities are at risk of displacement. IOM data show storms, drought, wildfires, extreme temperatures and floods forced nearly 30 million people from their homes in 2025. Pope said governments spend billions of dollars on border security while underfunding adaptation measures that could help communities remain in place. She estimated the cost of those measures at about $310 billion, compared with roughly $30 billion in funding so far. She argued that helping communities adapt before displacement occurs is more humane and cost-effective than responding to irregular migration after it begins.

items.title: [independent.co.uk] Super El Niño warms Pacific, threatens California marine life and snowpack
items.content_html: The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA) Climate Prediction Center said the developing El Niño is likely to remain strong to very strong through March 2027, with ocean temperatures still rising. The event is already associated with unusually warm waters off California, higher coastal water levels and changes in marine food supplies. Scientists report seabirds washing ashore and kelp forests under stress. The pattern can shift rainfall and temperature, and forecasters expect warmer winters in the Northwest that could reduce snowpack by raising snow levels. Scientists also warn that warm Pacific waters can increase the risk of coastal flooding when high tides coincide with storms. NOAA’s outlook says the event is expected to weaken early next year, while reports indicate its effects could continue into spring.

items.title: [gwec.net] Wind industry seeks faster permits and doubled investment to expand capacity
items.content_html: The Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), an industry group, and the Turkish Wind Energy Association launched a declaration at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya on Nov. 13, calling for faster wind development and outlining how global capacity could reach 4 terawatts by 2035. GWEC projects capacity will reach 2 terawatts by 2029 and 3 terawatts by 2035; reaching 4 terawatts would require stronger government support to reduce project risks and attract investment. The plan calls for predictable policies, faster permitting, upgraded grids, better access to finance and stronger supply chains. GWEC chief executive Ben Backwell said offshore wind farms can take two years to build but eight to 12 years to secure permits. Wind industry leaders also said doubling investment could lift annual capacity additions above 300 gigawatts.

items.title: [energynow.com] Norway’s Supreme Court invalidates three oilfield permits over emissions reviews
items.content_html: Norway’s Supreme Court on Nov. 13 invalidated government approvals for the North Sea oilfields Breidablikk, Tyrving and Yggdrasil, ruling that environmental reviews should have assessed emissions from burning the extracted oil, not just from production. The six-to-five decision requires the Energy Ministry to reconsider the permits under proper procedures but does not order operators to stop work. Equinor’s Breidablikk and Aker BP’s Tyrving are producing, and Yggdrasil is scheduled to start production in 2027. Environmental groups Greenpeace Norway and Young Friends of the Earth brought the case against the state in 2023. The court said the oil companies were not parties to the case, so the ruling does not automatically suspend their operations. The campaigners’ lawyer said they would consider bringing a separate case against the operators. The ministry said it would re-examine the permits. The government has said it has changed its practice to include emissions from burning oil and gas in assessments for new fields.

items.title: [japantimes.co.jp] Climate change intensified Indonesia’s worst wildfires in a decade, study finds
items.content_html: A World Weather Attribution study published Friday found that a strong El Niño drove Indonesia’s severe rainfall shortfall this year, while human-caused climate change made temperatures during the August-to-October fire season about 1.6 degrees Celsius higher. Researchers said warming made hot, dry fire conditions about three times more likely, while El Niño cut seasonal rainfall by roughly half. Decades of deforestation and peatland drainage also left the landscape more vulnerable to ignition. The fires have spread hazardous haze across Indonesia and neighboring Southeast Asian countries. Nusantara Atlas, an independent monitoring platform, estimated that fires affected 2.88 million hectares from January through October. The Indonesian government had not confirmed that total or issued its own estimate. Researchers called for peatland restoration, stronger land protections and reduced fossil-fuel emissions. Fires were still burning, with smoke detected in eastern Kalimantan on Nov. 12.

items.title: [gizmodo.com] Study finds Earth’s ice system beyond safe planetary limits
items.content_html: A study published in the journal Science on Nov. 12 finds that three parts of Earth’s cryosphere, or frozen regions — sea ice, snow cover and permafrost — have moved beyond the range considered safe for human societies, while land ice is on course to cross that boundary as warming continues. The researchers say these regions help regulate Earth’s energy, water and carbon cycles, and their decline increases the risks of sea-level rise, ecosystem damage and flooding. The team assessed four indicators against conditions over the past 11,700 years, when a relatively stable climate allowed human civilizations to develop. The researchers say the findings support urgent cuts to greenhouse-gas emissions and call for limits on black carbon and local disturbances such as industrial expansion. The authors released the paper during the COP31 climate conference and urged policymakers to use the proposed boundaries in climate planning.

The report also reviews fusion-plant concepts and the global network supporting their development, with a special focus on the data needed to apply artificial intelligence to fusion research.

items.title: [list.solar] Researchers report solar hydrogen production and faster panel recycling methods
items.content_html: Researchers at Switzerland’s EPFL developed an organic photocatalyst sheet that split water under simulated sunlight without an applied voltage, while a separate team demonstrated a method to rapidly separate photovoltaic module layers for recycling. EPFL’s device achieved about 0.1% solar-to-hydrogen efficiency and ran for more than two hours, but the researchers said its efficiency remains too low for practical use. The PV recycling method used induction heating to separate a test glass-to-glass module in as little as 5.4 seconds and recover 99.8% of its mass; the team next plans to test full-size commercial panels. Separately, Phys.org reported on a reusable molecular fabric that could reduce the energy required to separate industrial chemicals, but its article description gave no further technical details.

items.title: [world-nuclear-news.org] DOE clears Oklo’s Texas test reactor for unrestricted operations
items.content_html: The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) has cleared advanced nuclear company Oklo’s Groves-1 test reactor near Lockhart, Texas, for unrestricted operations, allowing it to begin research, equipment testing and staff training. The low-power reactor first achieved a self-sustaining chain reaction in August 2026, less than a year after construction began. Oklo plans to use operating data from Groves-1 to test capabilities for future isotope reactors and its Aurora fast-fission power plants and to refine engineering models. The company says benchmarking work could also inform fuel performance and power output in light-water reactors. The DOE authorization covers research and demonstration; commercial reactor designs still require review by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

items.title: [spravy.stvr.sk] AI data-center developers plan 181 GW of fossil-fuel power plants
items.content_html: Developers are proposing 181 gigawatts of fossil-fuel power plants beside planned AI data centers in the United States, Britain and continental Europe to avoid lengthy grid-connection delays, according to research firm BloombergNEF. If built, about 90% of the plants would be in the United States and produce an estimated 345 million metric tons of carbon-dioxide equivalent annually. BloombergNEF forecasts that AI data-center electricity demand will reach 2,354 terawatt-hours by 2035, nearly four times current levels and about 7% of global electricity use. Data-center electricity demand is growing faster than grid capacity, while households are covering part of the infrastructure costs. In the United States, data-center electricity demand has risen 19% a year since 2020, while grid capacity has expanded 2% annually. A separate estimate found that data centers covered only 38% of the $8.25 billion in grid costs associated with their growth in 2025, leaving residents to pay most of the remainder.

OPG has not yet provided a revised schedule or estimated the size of the overrun. It expects to substantially complete a cost-and-schedule assessment by mid-2027. items.title: [thesouthafrican.com] WMO warns strengthening El Niño could intensify global extremes into 2027
items.content_html: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says a strengthening El Niño could reach record strength by December and intensify heat and disruptive rainfall patterns into 2027. In its 2026 climate update, the agency reported that global temperatures from January through September averaged about 1.47°C above the preindustrial level and said 2026 is on track to rank among the four warmest years on record. Human-caused warming is adding to the risks associated with the naturally occurring climate pattern. The World Health Organization (WHO) has classified the expected health effects as an emergency for the first time for an El Niño event and published a plan for a Grade 3 preparedness response requiring major to maximal efforts. The agency warns that heat, drought and heavy rain can increase risks of heat illness, food insecurity and infectious disease, with vulnerable and conflict-affected communities facing particular danger. The WMO says the event is on track to reach record strength by December; its climate update uses data through September and does not include the latest impacts.

items.title: [apnews.com] Thunberg challenges COP31 leaders as talks target fossil-fuel transition
items.content_html: Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg returned to the United Nations climate summit for the first time since 2021, calling the COP31 negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, hypocritical and urging leaders to put people and the planet ahead of profits and geopolitical power. She said climate change threatens “everything and everyone we love” and accused fossil-fuel interests of influencing the talks. Delegates from nearly 200 countries are negotiating a proposed goal to increase electricity’s share of global energy use to 35% by 2035, from a little over one-fifth now. The Turkish proposal does not require the additional electricity to come from clean sources, while a broader plan to move away from coal, oil and gas remains unresolved. Turkey hosts the summit, while Australia leads the negotiations. The talks run through Nov. 20, with leaders’ speeches scheduled for Nov. 11 and 12. Negotiators are also working on climate finance and a just-transition mechanism. The United States is absent for a second consecutive year after President Donald Trump withdrew it from climate cooperation in 2025.

items.title: [indianexpress.com] India’s emissions rise 4.4% as major economies project declines
items.content_html: India’s fossil-fuel emissions are forecast to rise 4.4% in 2026, while the new Global Carbon Budget report projects a 0.4% decline worldwide. The report forecasts declines in China, the United States, the European Union and Japan. India’s projected increase exceeds its average annual growth of 3.5% over the past decade. The projected global decline is linked partly to reduced oil use after the Iran conflict disrupted supplies and drove up prices, as well as growth in renewable energy. India’s higher emissions are partly linked to increased demand for air conditioning and other cooling during an unusually hot, dry monsoon, according to one analysis. China’s emissions are projected to fall 0.9%. Pep Canadell, director of the Global Carbon Project, said China’s emissions had not grown over the past four years, but warned that a global peak still requires more renewable power, electric vehicles and industrial changes. The findings were released as countries meet at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya. Türkiye is pressing governments to raise electricity’s share of global energy demand to 35% by 2035, from about 20%. Critics say that target must be met with clean power to cut emissions.

🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Canadian Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin defended the government’s climate record before the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, citing methane action, electrification and international climate financing as evidence of Canada’s commitment to its targets. She is attending the conference’s first week, when activists expect other countries to question Canada’s recent policy shifts. The dispute centres on Ottawa’s unfulfilled 2021 pledge to ban thermal-coal exports: an environment commissioner’s report said work was abandoned in 2024 and formally ended in August 2025. Dabrusin said the previous government made the decision and her government is open to next steps. Climate advocates say continued exports undermine Canada’s leadership in the Powering Past Coal Alliance.

items.title: [eos.org] Arctic ice cores trace century-old toxic pollution to Montana mine
items.content_html:
🪶 🌲 🔭 ✏️

Researchers traced arsenic and other heavy metals preserved in 10 Arctic ice cores to the Anaconda Copper Mine in Montana, linking pollution to a single industrial source thousands of kilometers away. Arsenic levels in some cores reached about 15 times preindustrial levels around 1914, according to the study in Nature Sustainability. By combining ice-core measurements, atmospheric modeling and historical production records, the team estimated that about 50.5 million Americans and 600,000 Canadians were exposed to arsenic levels associated with increased health risks between 1898 and 1918. Pollution-control equipment installed at the smelter in 1919 reduced emissions by roughly 60% to 65%, though the mine continued operating until 1947. Lead researcher Joseph McConnell, a climate and environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, said epidemiologists should investigate the pollution’s potential effects on people.

items.title: [energymonitor.ai] Envision and ju:niz plan 442 MWh battery project in Germany
items.content_html: Envision Energy and German developer ju:niz Energy plan a 442-megawatt-hour battery storage project in Bavaria, one of several storage projects and product launches announced across Europe and Asia. The project, called Smareg 13, is the third under the companies’ partnership and would bring their joint portfolio to about 600 MWh. ju:niz will handle development, financing, construction and long-term operations. Other announcements include a 38-megawatt, 160-MWh project cluster in the Czech Republic for grid frequency regulation and electricity-market trading, and a 100-kWh solar-plus-storage system newly connected to the grid in Thailand. The announcements follow Chinese supplier Sungrow’s Australian distribution agreements for solar and battery products. Pylontech launched its Force Nex residential battery-inverter system in Australia and said it plans to introduce it in Europe and other global markets in the first quarter of 2027.
